3: Compute the result for a game of Hex / Polygon.
4: 
5: The abstract boardgame known as [Hex][hex] / Polygon / CON-TAC-TIX is quite simple in rules, though complex in practice.
6: Two players place stones on a parallelogram with hexagonal fields.
7: The player to connect his/her stones to the opposite side first wins.
8: The four sides of the parallelogram are divided between the two players (i.e. one player gets assigned a side and the side directly opposite it and the other player gets assigned the two other sides).
9: 
10: Your goal is to build a program that given a simple representation of a board computes the winner (or lack thereof).
11: Note that all games need not be "fair".
12: (For example, players may have mismatched piece counts or the game's board might have a different width and height.)
13: 
14: The boards look like this:
15: 
16: ```text
17: . O . X .
18:  . X X O .
19:   O O O X .
20:    . X O X O
21:     X O O O X
22: ```
23: 
24: "Player `O`" plays from top to bottom, "Player `X`" plays from left to right.
25: In the above example `O` has made a connection from left to right but nobody has won since `O` didn't connect top and bottom.

package connect

// ResultOf returns the winner of the game
func ResultOf(lines []string) (string, error) {
	board := make([][]byte, len(lines))
	for i, line := range lines {
		board[i] = []byte(line)
	}

	// X connects left to right
	if winner, ok := findWinner(board, 'X'); ok {
		return string(winner), nil
	}
	if winner, ok := findWinner(board, 'O'); ok {
		return string(winner), nil
	}
	return "", nil
}

func findWinner(board [][]byte, player byte) (byte, bool) {
	rows := len(board)
	cols := len(board[0])
	visited := make([][]bool, rows)
	for i := range visited {
		visited[i] = make([]bool, cols)
	}

	// BFS
	queue := [][2]int{}

	// For X, start from the left edge (col 0), for O, start from top edge (row 0)
	// This depends on the player

	if player == 'X' {
		// X starts from the left edge
		for r := 0; r < rows; r++ {
			if board[r][0] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{r, 0})
				visited[r][0] = true
			}
		}
	} else {
		// O starts from the top edge
		for c := 0; c < cols; c++ {
			if board[0][c] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{0, c})
				visited[0][c] = true
			}
		}
	}

	// neighbors
	// For X: (r, c-1), (r, c+1), (r-1, c), (r+1, c)
	// For O: (r, c-1), (r, c+1), (r-1, c-1), (r+1, c-1)

	for len(queue) > 0 {
		r, c := queue[0]
		queue = queue[1:]

		neighbors := [][2]int{}
		if player == 'X' {
			neighbors = [][2]int{{r, c - 1}, {r, c + 1}, {r - 1, c}, {r + 1, c}}
		} else {
			neighbors = [][2]int{{r, c - 1}, {r, c + 1}, {r - 1, c - 1}, {r + 1, c - 1}}
		}

		for _, n := range neighbors {
			nr, nc := n[0], n[1]
			if nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols {
				continue
			}
			if visited[nr][nc] || board[nr][nc] != player {
				continue
			}

			// Check if we reached the opposite edge
			if player == 'X' && nc == cols-1 {
				return player, true
			}
			if player == 'O' && nr == rows-1 {
				return player, true
			}

			visited[nr][nc] = true
			queue = append(queue, [2]int{nr, nc})
		}
	}

	return player, false
}

func findWinner(board [][]byte, player byte) (byte, bool) {
	rows := len(board)
	cols := len(board[0])

	visited := make([][]bool, rows)
	for i := range visited {
		visited[i] = make([]bool, cols)
	}

	queue := [][2]int{}

	if player == 'X' {
		for r := 0; r < rows; r++ {
			if board[r][0] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{r, 0})
				visited[r][0] = true
			}
		}
	} else {
		for c := 0; c < cols; c++ {
			if board[0][c] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{0, c})
				visited[0][c] = true
			}
		}
	}

	for len(queue) > 0 {
		r, c := queue[0]
		queue = queue[1:]

		neighbors := [][2]int{}
		if player == 'X' {
			neighbors = [][2]int{{r, c - 1}, {r, c + 1}, {r - 1, c}, {r + 1, c}}
		} else {
			neighbors = [][2]int{{r, c - 1}, {r, c + 1}, {r - 1, c - 1}, {r + 1, c - 1}}
		}

		for _, n := range neighbors {
			nr, nc := n[0], n[1]
			if nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols {
				continue
			}
			if visited[nr][nc] || board[nr][nc] != player {
				continue
			}

			if player == 'X' && nc == cols-1 {
				return player, true
			}
			if player == 'O' && nr == rows-1 {
				return player, true
			}

			visited[nr][nc] = true
			queue = append(queue, [2]int{nr, nc})
		}
	}

	return player, false
}

package connect

// ResultOf returns the winner of the game.
// Player "X" connects from the left edge to the right edge.
// Player "O" connects from the top edge to the bottom edge.
func ResultOf(lines []string) (string, error) {
	board := make([][]byte, len(lines))
	for i, line := range lines {
		board[i] = []byte(line)
	}

	if winner, ok := findWinner(board, 'X'); ok {
		return string(winner), nil
	}
	if winner, ok := findWinner(board, 'O'); ok {
		return string(winner), nil
	}
	return "", nil
}

// findWinner reports whether player has connected their two assigned edges.
func findWinner(board [][]byte, player byte) (byte, bool) {
	rows := len(board)
	if rows == 0 {
		return player, false
	}
	cols := len(board[0])
	if cols == 0 {
		return player, false
	}

	visited := make([][]bool, rows)
	for i := range visited {
		visited[i] = make([]bool, cols)
	}

	queue := [][2]int{}

	// Seed the search from the player's starting edge.
	if player == 'X' {
		// X starts from the left edge (column 0).
		for r := 0; r < rows; r++ {
			if board[r][0] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{r, 0})
				visited[r][0] = true
			}
		}
	} else {
		// O starts from the top edge (row 0).
		for c := 0; c < cols; c++ {
			if board[0][c] == player {
				queue = append(queue, [2]int{0, c})
				visited[0][c] = true
			}
		}
	}

	// The six neighbours of a cell in the hexagonal grid.
	neighbors := [][2]int{
		{0, -1}, {0, 1},
		{-1, 0}, {-1, 1},
		{1, -1}, {1, 0},
	}

	for len(queue) > 0 {
		r, c := queue[0]
		queue = queue[1:]

		for _, d := range neighbors {
			nr, nc := r+d[0], c+d[1]
			if nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols {
				continue
			}
			if visited[nr][nc] || board[nr][nc] != player {
				continue

- The win check happens on dequeue (not just for neighbors), which correctly handles the 1×1 board where the start and end edges coincide.

The key subtlety I verified by hand was that the **same** six-neighbor adjacency works for both players — only the start/end edges differ. A player-specific 4-neighbor scheme (a common shortcut) fails the "O wins top to bottom" case, so I used the full hexagonal neighborhood.
